Kaiser Permanente is pleased
Kaiser Permanente writes that the change to a 10-day follow-up appointment standard for non-physician MH providers locks in a return interval not tied to clinical judgement. Return appointments for MH and SUD should meet individual patient needs and be deemed medically indicated by the patient's treating provider. This mandate will lead to an increase in caseloads for mental health therapists, which Kaiser Permanente and other health systems must manage. A primary and fundamental challenge is to build the workforce necessary to meet the current demand for MH care. As the UCSF San Francisco benchmark study of the mental health care workforce illustrates, we face a MH workforce shortage crisis in California. In 2018, UCSF noted that without concerted effort California will have 50% fewer psychiatrists and nearly 30% fewer therapists than we need to meet patterns of demand for behavioral health services by 2028. Forty-five percent of psychiatrists and 37% of psychologists will be approaching retirement age in that same period. Kaiser Permanente concludes that the COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated the shortage we were already facing, as demand for MH care has greatly increased

The California Association of Health Facilities (CAHF) writes that it
The California Association of Health Plans (CAHP), the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC), and America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP), write that under the ACA, states are required to select an essential health benefit (EHB) plan that defines the health-related services and equipment that health plans and insurance policies must cover. The benchmark plan selected by the Legislature in California did not include hearing aids. CHBRP has confirmed that coverage for hearing aids and associated services mandated by this proposal would exceed EHBs, and therefore trigger the ACA requirement that the state defray the cost of additional benefit coverage for enrollees in QHPs in Covered California. CHBRP estimates that this bill could translate to a state-responsibility of $11,268,000 annually. It's also important to note that this would be the first time since the passage of the ACA that California could pass a coverage mandate that exceeds the EHBs. The opposition is concerned about the precedent that this action may set, which could trigger a slew of new mandates to be introduced that exceed the EHBs, requiring more state funding to defray these costs. Additionally, this mandate is projected to cost enrollees approximately $52 million in increased premiums. CAHP, ACLHIC, and AHIP are also concerned about this bill's potential to harm affordability for small businesses and individual market consumers
The California Association of Health Plans and Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies state this bill unnecessarily codifies a current treatment practice that is already considered a covered benefit when it is determined to be medically necessary

Additional enforcement tools required Similar to the investor protections discussed in Comment 2(a), the enforcement tools contained in the bill appear to be arguably incomplete given the potential for serious financial damage if an issuer violates the requirements of the exemption. For example, it appears arguably appropriate for any issuer using the proposed exception to bear the burden of proof to demonstrate that the offering or sale complied with the requirements described above. From a policy standpoint, placing the burden on the issuer is arguably appropriate since that person or entity chose to use the exemption, without oversight, and essentially self- certified that the exemption's requirements were met. Furthermore, given the lack of oversight, it appears appropriate to enact strong penalties to deter any issuer who contemplates violating the proposed investor protections, and to ensure individuals who are the victims of fraud are able to seek appropriate relief for those bad acts. Accordingly, the Committee should consider the following amendments to improve the enforcement measures and remedies available to an investor: • provide that the issuer (who used the exemption) has the burden of proof to demonstrate that the offering complied with the requirements of the exemption

Possible Remedies for Commercial and Business (Wayne) PageK ? Civil Court Complaints for Individuals Who Post Defamatory Messages or Infringe Trade Secrets. In addition to the proposed statutory changes contemplated by this bill, there are potential civil court actions that may provide some relief to victims of deceptive electronic communications. According to published news accounts, the first corporate lawsuit to go to trial against defendants for posting caustic messages on message boards resulted in a $775,000 damages award to Varian Medical Systems. (Varian Medical Systems v. Delfino, Santa Clara Co. 780187.) Many companies have filed civil complaints against individuals who post messages, alleging the information is defamatory or infringes trade secrets. The Delfino case involved a number of different allegations, including the posting of messages impersonating company officials and messages calling employees of the defendant liars, sexually promiscuous or mentally unstable. In addition, the trial judge issued a permanent injunction against the defendants posting certain information. Depending on the facts, aggrieved parties may also have a remedy pursuant to Business and Professions Code Section 17538.4, a statute that was amended in 1998 to regulate transmitting unsolicited advertising by electronic mail. The Court of Appeal in Ferguson v. Friendfinders, Inc. (2002) 94 Cal. App. 4th 1255, held that the statute does not violate the Commerce Clause of the United States Constitution. Civil Code section 1709 includes a cause of action for fraud. This action lies where a person deceives another with intent to induce the other person to alter his or her position to his or her detriment. 5. Additional Background About Stock Manipulation by Spoofing - This Practice is Difficult to Stop - Issues of Federal Law Congressman John Dingell wrote a letter quoted below concerning stock manipulation through "spoofing" or the entry PageL of "phantom quotes." The December 12, 1999, New York Times article "Chasing Ghosts at Nasdaq," that sparked my original inquiry, suggested that the parties putting in phantom quotes may be taking advantage of market structure reforms sponsored by the SEC over the last few years that have given small investors increased opportunities to have their orders reflected in the quotations of market makers and the trading systems known as ECNs. While these reforms have provided both large and small investors increased flexibility and cost savings, it is also true that the improved market access can be "gamed" in a manipulative manner. I applaud your efforts to improve capacity and surveillance and to prosecute offenders so that consumers are protected and the nation's securities markets remain efficient, fair, and honest. (Emphasis added.) The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday, June 12, 2002, published an article about an on-line news service that published a hoax news release about a drug company. The incident was referred to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The story noted that stopping such false communications was extremely difficult. The story stated: "Someone duped Internet Wire into publishing a phony [press] release about Cel-Sci Corp. on Monday, causing at least a short-lived jump in the drug company's stock. The release has since been retracted, although Internet Wire and Cel-Sci say they don't yet know who is behind the false release." A copyright story published on August 23, 2001, in the Seattle Times noted described a form of spoofing in the stock markets: The National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD) PageM is investigating 11 cases of possible "spoofing" by brokers who try to manipulate stock prices by entering false quotes and then canceling them. Traders' use of these so-called "phantom quotes" has persisted even as regulators have tightened surveillance of the Nasdaq Stock Market and filed charges against seven brokers and investors since 1998, NASD Executive Vice President Stephen Luparello said in an interview. The NASD, a self-policing brokers' group, also has referred 21 other possible spoofing cases for Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry in the last 2-1/2 years, including two this past May, he said. "The integrity of the market suffers from this practice because the quotes indicate that something might be happening with a stock when it's really just manipulation," Luparello said. Spoofing, which can be considered fraud, typically occurs on thinly traded Nasdaq stocks with wide spreads, Luparello said. 6. Constitutional Issues - Particularly First Amendment Concerns Concerns have been raised about creating a new crime that would punish knowingly sending a false e-mail or other electronic communication with the intent to injure, particularly in light of the wide interpretation given the term injury in the crime of sending a false telephone or telegraph message as defined in Penal Code section 474. Of particular concern is possible effect of this new crime on the exercise of free speech rights protected by the First Amendment. This is especially true in regard to speech involving parody and sharp political criticism

Current structure reflects historical needs of an agrarian society of limited mobility This amendment proposes a monumental change in the structure of justice in California, but is actually reflective of a trend toward consolidation and unification that has been growing for some time. Fiscal restraints and technological advances have encouraged judges and court administrators to seek out more efficient methods of conducting the court's business which suggest that the historical divisions among superior and inferior tribunals may be obsolete. The current jurisdictional arrangement of the trial courts arise from common law tradition, from the county courts and hundreds of medieval England through the structure common to the United States at California's admission: a court of general jurisdiction in each county to deal with consequential matters (felonies, civil actions involving substantial prayers), and justices of the peace in each locale to handle magisterial duties, minor violations of the law, and equitable resolutions of minor civil disputes. With the first State Constitution of 1849, trial jurisdiction was divided among district courts (equivalent to superior courts but not divided along county lines), county courts (handling probate and appeals from the justices' courts), and justices of the peace (Art. VI). The superior court in California dates to the Constitution of 1879)

ARGUMENTS IN SUPPPORT: According to the author, "California is in the midst of an unprecedented housing crisis caused by a severe lack of new housing construction at all levels of affordability. Passed in 1982, the Housing Accountability Act (HAA) has served for more 30 years as a tool to ensure that municipalities do not unfairly hinder the development of new housing projects, and to ensure new housing construction during crises like the one California faces today. Under the HAA, local governments must follow certain legal mandates before denying a housing development application that complies with their general plan and zoning rules. Unfortunately, the current enforcement mechanisms of the HAA are inadequate to achieve compliance in many cases. One of the most significant barriers to the construction of new housing is unjustified local resistance from NIMBY (Not in My Backyard) groups. In a recent report, the Legislative Analyst's Office confirmed that new housing construction faces community opposition, "because it often is perceived as bringing negative changes to a community's quality or character." Using these types of unreasonable arguments, "no growth advocates" and NIMBYs have significantly curtailed housing construction, which significantly worsens the jobs-housing imbalance in our communities, in contravention to state law. This imbalance causes hardship for many people, especially low-income families in need of housing close to their jobs. Building more infill housing and reducing lengthy commute times are also necessary for California to achieve its ambitious 2030 greenhouse gas reduction target, as enumerated in SB 32

Activities involving the agent's willful misuse of public funds, willful breach of fiduciary duty, or willful or corrupt misconduct in office
Activities involving the agent's willful omission to perform his or her official duty. With this definition of "improper governmental activity," concerns raised earlier by groups such as the California County Counsels Association and the California Association of Sanitation Agencies have been addressed. However, the Attorney General is still concerned about the potential harmful effect of allowing disclosure of what would otherwise be privileged information between attorney and client under the aegis of "improper governmental activity." The definition of the phrase (which earlier included phrases drawn from Rule 3-600, such as "a violation of law reasonably imputable to the organization"), the Attorney General argues, leaves the interpretation of what is improper governmental activity to the individual attorney and his or her personal and political views. "While we may all agree that certain conduct, such as the Quackenbush mis-administration (sic) of the Department of Insurance, should see the light of day, we may have legitimate differences of opinion about whether a governmental activity is "likely to result in substantial injury to the organization," involves "willful misuse of public funds" or "breach of fiduciary duty," or involves the "willful omission to perform" an official duty. The proposed exceptions?will unwisely empower attorneys representing public agencies to act as free agents subject to their personal viewpoint, and place them in a state of perpetual conflict with their clients, chilling the trust and open access to information essential to their profession and compromising their effectiveness." [Letter from the Attorney General's Office, dated June 27, 2002.] The Attorney General suggests limiting the definition of "improper governmental activity" to "conduct that constitutes or would constitute a felony." With this definition, the AG states, there would be little difference between attorneys in interpretation of conduct that should clearly be reported. The Attorney General makes a good point. A broad definition might embolden publicity-seeking disclosures by loose cannons, to the detriment of the government agency. However, their suggested amendment may narrow the bill too much. For example, it is not clear if an agency official who used a government charge card to purchase a personal item during official travel is guilty of a felony. A possible consequence of that narrow amendment is a spate of future legislative measures to upgrade current misdemeanors to felonies, just to protect the government attorney whistleblower. There are other phrases used in the Government Code that also may be used to limit these exceptions to the attorney-client confidentiality rule, such as conduct that is "willful or corrupt misconduct in office" that would be grounds for removal of a public official from office. [Government Code Section 3060 et seq.] This phrase has been extensively interpreted in case law to apply to situations that would appear to be "improper governmental activity" as defined by , although the situations are limited to local agency officials, including school district officials. has been amended to remove from the definition of "improper governmental activity" undefined violations of law "reasonably imputable to the organization" or "likely to cause substantial injury to the organization," which, under Rule 3-600, could trigger an attorney representing an organization to take actions consistent with Section 6068(e) or, if necessary, resign. Thus "improper government activity" includes conduct that is less definitive than a felony, as the Attorney General would prefer, but would fall under "willful or corrupt misconduct in office," "willful or breach of fiduciary duty," "willful misuse of public funds," and conduct constituting "crime, fraud, or serious and willful violations of law." In all of the above cases, the improper governmental activity should probably be tied to substantial harm to the public interest, so that the attorney would be compelled to take the protected actions in order to prevent or rectify the improper governmental activity. SHOULD THE IMPROPER GOVERNMENTAL ACTIVITY CONSTITUTE CONDUCT THAT, IF NOT PREVENTED OR RECTIFIED, WOULD CAUSE SUBSTANTIAL HARM TO THE PUBLIC INTEREST? Where the conduct of the governmental organization meets one or more of those defined as "improper governmental activity" under , an attorney would be faced with the choice of taking several actions. b. First order of action: urge reconsideration and/or go to highest internal authority Under this bill, an attorney who learns of improper governmental activity in the course of representing a governmental organization may take one or both actions specified by Rule 3-600 (B)(1) [urge reconsideration of the matter while explaining its likely consequences to the organization] and (2) [refer the matter to the highest internal authority if warranted]. These actions would be subject to the Section 6068(e) rule of confidentiality, as they are under current law. By specifying the actions that an attorney may take when he or she learns of improper governmental activity, establishes a clear path of action for the attorney to take, rather than a broad spectrum of undefined actions that could be proper under Rule 3-600 (those actions that are "in the best, lawful interest of the organization"). This is an important precursor to the next, more serious level of action that an attorney may take, when warranted. c. Second order of action: refer matter to law enforcement agency or official with oversight authority over governmental organization or official In limited cases, would allow the attorney to take further action, notwithstanding the attorney's duty to maintain confidence of the client under Section 6068(e), under any one of three scenarios: 1) if the attorney has taken both actions (urging reconsideration and referring to a higher authority in the organization without the matter getting resolved

CONCERNS. Anthem Blue Cross (Anthem) states that this bill sets up an Exchange framework that is inconsistent with the concept of consumer choice by requiring the exchange to "determine health benefits." Furthermore, Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes benefit tiers and "essential health benefits" for the individual and small employer markets, whether coverage is purchased inside or outside the Exchange, and that having the Exchange "determine and approve benefit designs" is duplicative of federal requirements and will only serve to further limit consumer choice. Anthem writes that this bill makes the Exchange an "active purchaser," thus allowing it to set prices. Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes a rate review process for premiums charged in the individual and small group markets, which will be executed by the CDI and DMHC. Anthem states that if both the regulators and the Exchange are responsible for approving rates without a consistent process, the rates for the same product could be different inside and outside of the Exchange, violating the federal requirement that the entire market be treated as a single risk pool. Finally, Anthem asserts that setting rates in the Exchange would likely politicize the rate- setting process, which has proven to lead to insurer insolvency and insurers withdrawing from the market, reducing choices for consumers. Anthem suggests amending this bill to remove these provisions and instead clarifying that regulation of health plan and insurance products sold through the exchange are the sole purview of the CDI and DMHC. The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC) writes that the Exchange appears to have the power to negotiate rates for the products sold within the Exchange, and at the same time, requires participating carriers to offer the same products outside the Exchange. ACLHIC is concerned that these negotiated rates may not be actuarially sound and place participating carriers at a market disadvantage with nonparticipating carriers. ACLHIC states that participating carriers should compete on quality and price. ACLHIC also writes that there is already extensive criteria for carrier certification to participate in an Exchange included in PPACA, and will be further expanded when federal rules come forward, and that additional and potentially conflicting state standards may serve to limit the choice of plan in the Exchange. ACLHIC argues that, given the robust certification criteria that will already apply, any carrier that can meet those criteria should be eligible to participate in the Exchange. The California Hospital Association (CHA) is concerned over the provision in this bill that specifically expand the role of County Organized Health Systems beyond the original scope and purpose. CHA states that without a compelling reason to do so, it could be premature to provide for government-operated health plans to offer commercial coverage in the private health insurance market

California's wiretap statute makes it a felony to intercept wire and electronic communications except for a narrow list of crimes. California's wiretap statute provides more privacy protections for ordinary, law-abiding persons than is currently provided for under federal law. There are substantial internal checks within law enforcement, district attorney offices and the courts to ensure that wiretap orders are only approved when there is probable cause to suspect that one of the enumerated offenses is being committed and that alternative methods of investigation and detection have been exhausted. Narcotics wiretaps allow law enforcement to disrupt and dismantle drug trafficking organizations in Southern California. Compensation Insurance Fund is statutorily exempt from the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act and the California Public Records Act
Compline provides this information in a user-friendly, electronic format on a subscription basis to hundreds of insurance agents and brokers in California. As existing law does not provide for information service companies to have direct access to ex-mod information gathered by the WCIRB, Compline's current source of ex-mod information is through admitted workers' compensation insurers. These insurers are statutorily required to share information on their policyholders with the WCIRB, and, in turn, they can access, in hard copy, WCIRB's consolidated statewide data concerning employer ex-mods and related information. The sponsors state that this bill is necessary in light of plans by the WCIRB to institute a new, on-line system that will allow the WCIRB to provide information, including ex-mod information, electronically to member insurers and agents and brokers who subscribe to the system. This new system is very similar to the system that information service companies currently have in place. The sponsors argue that unless information service companies, such as Compline, can obtain the same information, in the same format and at the same time as the WCIRB intends to release it, information service companies will be unable to compete. The result, sponsors contend, will be that the WCIRB, a quasi-public entity created to collect, compile and analyze data required to be submitted to it from every admitted workers' compensation insurer, will be the exclusive provider of ex-mod information and other related information. The sponsors assert that establishing the WCIRB as the sole provider of this information was not the Legislature's intent, nor was it their intent to allow the WCIRB to develop an exclusive for-profit franchise to sell information to workers' compensation insurance agents and brokers. The sponsors argue that this bill will maintain a competitive market in the business of providing access to workers' compensation ex-mod and other related information, which is used by insurance agents and brokers to facilitate the placement of workers' compensation insurance on behalf of their clients. Without this legislation, the sponsors assert that competition in providing access to this information will be drastically reduced or eliminated

In addition to being duplicative of existing protections, the bill also will place an impediment on the sale of wells. In today's oil and gas industry, purchasers of wells are often operators committed to continuing California operations and who are aware of their plugging obligations. Sellers tend to be operators who are looking to relocate, divest, or simply exit the oil and gas production business. By prohibiting the use of blanket bonds to satisfy bonding requirements associated with a new acquisition, this bill sets an impediment to purchases. When a seller cannot find a purchaser for their well, that seller is now trapped. As other costs of operations increase, the probability increases that the owner who had wanted to sell the well or wells will become insolvent

Injury and death by firearm are consistently the most common method of suicide both in the United States and in California, accounting for nearly half of suicides committed. According to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), self-inflicted injury and suicide by firearm accounted for 4.1 deaths per 100,000 residents in 2017. The use of firearm for self-inflicted injury and suicide result in lethal outcomes in nearly every instance. Further, rates of suicide vary significantly throughout California, both demographically and geographically. Northern rural California residents are significantly more likely to commit suicide than urban or suburban residents, and rates of suicide among older men were nearly five times as high as the rate for all age groups between 1999 and 2016. Suicide by firearm among California men is also consistently higher than women. White and Native American Californians were also found to commit suicide by firearm at disproportionately higher rates than other racial and ethnic groups. Currently, information on suicide prevention resources is not available at any point in process of obtaining a firearm. The decision to commit suicide is often made in a short timeframe with research showing that an overwhelming majority of individuals who have survived a suicide attempt acted on the ideation within one hour. Suicide prevention labeling, signage, and educational information, as proposed in this measure, is a promising step toward empowering Californians with preventive health and safety information to receive services and support in times of crisis

Motorcycle helmets save lives. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) requires that all motorcycle helmets sold in the United States meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) 218. This standard defines minimum levels of performance that helmets must meet to protect the head and brain in the event of a crash. According to NHTSA, helmets that do not meet FMVSS 218 create a higher risk for skull fracture and brain injury when compared to certified ones. Approval of a helmet model that does not comply with rigorous federal safety standards will undoubtedly impact public safety

These findings and observations are consistent with the results of on-line sting operations, including sweeps of networking sites. Recent legislation established the Marine Life Management Act (MLMA) which gives DFG the authority and a mandate to develop a management and resource enhancement program for any fishery regulated at the time MLMA became effective, which would include the sea urchin fishery. MLMA first required DFG to develop a management plan for the fin fishery, and then the white sea bass fishery, and then prioritize the other fisheries for future management efforts, and report those priorities to the Legislature this Fall. It is expected that the sea urchin fishery will be one of the top priorities in that report. If so, there is a potential conflict between the authority of the Sea Urchin Advisory Committee under this bill and the mandate DFG will be under pursuant to the MLMA. The Natural Resources Committee may wish to inquire of the author and DFG how this potential conflict may be resolved. 2 DFG, as well as many other state agencies, have at times been criticized for being "too close" to the industries they are supposed to be regulating. This bill seems to turn this concern on its head by giving greater authority to the sea urchin industry to protect the public's interest in maintaining a healthy sea urchin fishery. Responding to the concerns of opponents, the author recently amended the bill to require that grand jury proceedings be open only when testimony under oath is being given. The author further amended the bill to permit the grand jury, through a joint request with the attorney general or the district attorney, to close the grand jury proceedings to the public when necessary, subject to the approval by the presiding judge of the superior court. The author of the bill states that this measure will "[promote] accuracy and thoroughness in grand jury proceedings." Witness' Proposed Right to Counsel: As noted above, this bill would also allow a witness before a civil grand jury proceeding who is or becomes the subject of a grand jury investigation to have an attorney present under specified conditions during his or her testimony. This section of the bill is identical to an earlier measure, AB 527 (Baugh), which was passed by the Legislature in 1999, but then vetoed by the governor. Proponents of the measure contend that in the absence of having counsel present an uninformed witness may inadvertently waive his or her essential rights, or may hesitate to testify entirely because of fear of being without guidance. Existing law prohibits the attorney for a witness to be present during his or her testimony before the grand jury. The only persons who are allowed to be present during grand jury proceedings are members of the grand jury, prosecutors, and necessary personnel such as a court reporter and an interpreter. (Section 939.) While the attorney for a witness is prohibited from being present during a client's testimony, witnesses before the grand jury do have a right to confer with counsel during the proceedings. The counsel waits outside the hearing room and any time the witness wants to confer with counsel he or she is permitted to do so. Commenting on the impracticality of this practice, the author of the bill highlights: Often the witness will have retained counsel, but counsel must remain outside the room resulting in an almost comedic routine of the jurors asking a question, the witness leaving the room to consult with counsel, and then returning to answer the question. The United States Supreme Court has stated that the constitutional right to counsel attaches at the initiation of adversary proceedings. (Kirby v. Illinois, 406 U.S. 682, 688 (U.S. 1972).) The Court noted that, "the right to counsel exists to protect the accused during trial-type confrontations with the prosecutor." (United States v. Gouveia, 467 U.S. 180, 190 (U.S. 1984).) The California Supreme Court addressed concern over the potential for abuse of the grand jury process, noting: "The prosecuting attorney is typically in complete control of the total process in the grand jury room: he calls the witnesses, interprets the evidence, states and applies the law, and advises the grand jury on whether a crime has been committed. The grand jury is independent only in the sense that it is not formally attached to the prosecutor's office

Retroactive Benefits: PEPRA specifically prohibits the provision of retroactive pension benefits. The affected judges have been in the PEPRA plan for approximately five years. This bill, as currently written, would place them into the pre-PEPRA plan effective from their 2012 membership date. This would result in a return of contributions and an eventual higher pension allowance based on one year of final compensation instead of three-year final compensation. Together, these effects would be a retroactive enhancement since the judges would pay less for their pension benefits while receiving an increased pension allowance

When Governor Davis vetoed this proposal contained in AB 527 in 1999, he stated: The current operation of the grand jury, which follows English common law practice, has remained essentially unchanged since California was admitted to the Union in 1850 and has served us well for 150 years... Thus, any major departures from existing practice warrants thorough and thoughtful consideration and debate within the legal community and among legal scholars. In response to the governor's veto, legal scholars at the "Capital Center" noted above conducted a study on the potential reform of California's grand jury system. (Vitiello & Kelso, Reform of California's Grand Jury System, supra at 515.) At the conclusion of its study the Capital Center observed (supportive of the merits of this provision in the measure): Counsel has a role in assuring that a target makes proper invocation of such [constitutional] rights and privileges. Counsel may also encourage some targets to testify. This offers the grand jury a fuller understanding of the facts than might otherwise have been available. The end result increases the grand jury's ability to exercise independent judgment on whether to indict. . . . [T]he creation of the right to counsel furthers independence of the grand jury and . . . serves the public's interest, and not merely the interest of the target. Additionally, twenty years prior to Governor Davis' veto of AB 527 the American Bar Association (ABA) conducted an investigation of the grand jury system, concluding after several years of study that "a witness before the grand jury shall have the right to be accompanied by counsel in his or her appearance before the grand jury." (American Bar Association, Grand Jury Policy and Model Act (1977-1982) (Marcia Christensen ed., 2d ed. 1982) [hereinafter ABA Report].) The ABA commented that limiting the role of counsel would prevent the grand jury from becoming a "mini-trial," but would address concerns about the unfairness of disallowing a witness from being accompanied by counsel. The ABA study went on to observe: Requiring a witness who needs advice of counsel to consult his attorney outside the grand jury room door is awkward and prejudicial. It unnecessarily prolongs the grand jury proceedings and places the witness in an unfavorable light before the grand jurors. The American Law Institute has called it a "degrading and irrational" procedure. It is extremely damaging to the witness continually to get up, go outside, and consult with counsel. This sentiment was reflected in the testimony of former Watergate Special Prosecutor Charles Ruff when he testified before the House Judiciary Subcommittee in 1977, declaring: The mere possibility of occasional disruption simply cannot overcome the right of the individual witness to consult his attorney without going through the mildly absurd process of leaving the grand jury room every time. Indeed, most prosecutors would admit, I think, that they count on the burden of leaving the room to dissuade the witness from asserting his right to counsel." (Testimony before House Judiciary Subcommittee, April 27, 1977, at 3.) Allowing Witnesses to Have an Attorney Present During Grand Jury Testimony Would Put California In Line with the Practices of Other States: A state- by-state study conducted by the United States Department of Justice, and later updated by the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) reveals that twenty-one states, including Arkansas, Colorado, Utah, Nevada, Florida, New York, and Kansas allow some witnesses to have counsel present during grand jury proceedings. (NACDL, State by State Information Sheet¸ available at http://www.nacdl.org/grandjury. Furthermore, this proposed section of the measure appears to conform to the recommendations of the American Bar Association, put forth in a comment to a Judicial Advisory Committee of the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. Kansas additionally permits counsel to interpose objections. Calls for similar reform to allow witnesses the right to have counsel present during testimony have been echoed by the Cato Institute, the Capital Center for Government Law and Policy, and others
See, 15 USC 1312(i)(7). "Any person compelled to appear under a demand for oral testimony pursuant to this section may be accompanied, represented, and advised by counsel

Supporters of this bill, largely organizations that support children's health and recreation, cite federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention findings that drowning among California's children ages one to four years is the leading cause of accidental deaths and the second leading cause of death for those ages five to nine years. Despite changes to the law, California has experienced an increase in fatal drownings among young children in recent years. Over 70% of near drownings occur in residential swimming pools, with many of the children experiencing lifelong disabilities. Supporters further argue that a 2020 report from California's Department of Developmental Services reported a caseload of 768 individuals requiring lifelong services because of near drownings, representing significant long-term costs to the state. Supporters of this bill concur with the national American Academy of Pediatrics' strong recommendation that the state establish a systematic reporting process on the circumstances of drownings to develop best practices, community interventions, and specific public policies addressing this critical issue

The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC) and the California Association of Health Plans (CAHP) write that their
The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC), and the California Association of Health Plans (CAHP), write that similar policies have been attempted in other states without the desired results. For example, the OCCP was enacted by the Oregon state legislature during the 2013 session SB 604 (Anderson) of 2013. ACLHIC and CAHP write that the biggest concern is that this bill would prevent any healthcare entity from imposing additional criteria which may be determined based on quality or risk assessment. Further, there is also language that states, "This section does not prohibit a health care service plan or health insurer, or its delegated entity, from using another credentialing process or procedure." Plans presume this only comes into play if the provider does not want to use the certified credentialing entity. But it is not clear what would be allowed with this flexibility. Furthermore, allowing for more than one credentialing entity could lead to inconsistency. Providers could forum shop until they find an entity that will credential them. Even if these entities utilize the same standards, there is still likely to be inconsistency in credentialing decisions if there are different decision makers. Which regulatory body will ensure the credentialing entity covers all applicable credentialing criteria required? Will the board ensure that verification expiration dates are the same as other standards and basic credentialing requirements? Also, will the verifications be performed at the time of the request from a health plan? If the health plans are forced to accept the credentialing of an outside entity, will that entity bear the risk of a negligent credentialing action? Or will the plan be indemnified in some way? What about adverse providers (i.e. providers with quality issues, adverse actions, criminal records)? Who will determine the quality criteria for certifying adverse providers? Lastly, without a uniform database, how would plans obtain the provider data for these providers? What liability would providers be willing to assume for an accurate up to date database for streamlined credentialing
The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies, America's Health Insurance Plans, and California Association of Health Plans write that the benchmark plan selected by the Legislature in California did not include hearing aids. CHBRP has confirmed that coverage for hearing aids and associated services mandated by this proposal would exceed EHBs, and therefore trigger the ACA requirement that the state defray the cost of additional benefit coverage for enrollees in qualified health plans in Covered California. CHBRP estimates that this bill could translate to a state-responsibility of $11,268,000 annually. It's also important to note that this would be the first time since the passage of the ACA that California could pass a coverage mandate that exceeds the EHBs. Health plans and insurers are concerned about the precedent that this action may set, which could trigger a slew of new mandates to be introduced that exceed the EHBs, requiring more state funding to defray these costs. Additionally, this mandate is projected to cost enrollees approximately $52 million in increased premiums. Health plans and insurers are also concerned about this bill's potential to harm affordability for small businesses and individual market consumers

The California Association of Dental Plans (CADP) writes dental waiting period provisions are predominately used in the individual dental plan market where enrollees pay their own premium, whereas pre-existing "missing tooth" exclusions are used across individual and group markets. A dental waiting period is a set time ranging from six to 12 months before an enrollee can receive full coverage for specific categories of dental procedures - usually, major dental care. However, CADP notes, individual dental plans cover diagnostic and preventive dental care without any waiting period. CADP points out the individual dental market primarily serves low and middle income Californians without access to dental coverage through their employer, with limited excess funds for dental premiums. CADP contends actuarial analysis of existing dental plans in this market indicates elimination of waiting periods would increase premiums 45% on plans with a six-month waiting period

The California Association of Health Plans, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies, and America's Health Insurance Plans (collectively "opposition") write that drug manufacturers acknowledge their drugs are unaffordable for patients, but rather than choose to lower their prices for everyone, they point to their PAPs, which offer copay coupons. PAPs offer coupons only to a narrow set of patients, for a narrow selection of drugs, and often only for a limited time. Once the patient hits their deductible, drugmakers discontinue the patient's coupons. The opposition argues this scheme allows drugmakers to keep their underlying prices hidden from patients, while keeping their costs extremely high for employers and consumers who end up paying much more in premiums and cost-sharing. The opposition notes that the federal government considers copay coupons illegal kickbacks in federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid because these coupons induce a patient to use a specific drug. To counter the market manipulation from coupons, health plans and insurers have worked together with employers to develop programs to hold drug companies accountable, to shed light on these pricing schemes, and keep costs low for Californians. Such programs help restore the balance in the system by allowing patients to use manufacturer coupons to save money at the pharmacy counter, but does not count the amount the drug manufacturer has paid for the drug (through the coupon) towards the patient's deductible or OOP maximum. The opposition argues legislation like this bill that bans these programs by requiring health plans and insurers to count third-party payments towards an enrollee's cost sharing obligations will eliminate incentives for drug companies to lower prices. The opposition concludes that as a result, drug companies will make more money while California families and businesses continue to foot the bill through higher premiums, higher OOP expenses, and higher federal insurance subsidies
The California Association of Health Plans, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies, and America's Health Insurance Plans write this bill negates the health plan's or insurer's ability to ensure clinically appropriate use of prescription drugs, and encourages the use of expensive specialty and brand name drugs when a generic or lower cost brand equivalent is available and clinically appropriate. The opponents state that when health plans and insurers limit or deny a drug or specific dose of a drug, it is generally for safety reasons, such as potential abuse or overuse, inconsistency with FDA-approved labeling, or to prevent use at doses that have not been shown to be efficacious. Lastly, opponents argue this bill will lead to potentially dramatic increases in health care costs in California, largely because this bill prohibits plans from adjusting the enrollee or insured's portion of the cost share if the drug had previously been covered, regardless of an increase in dosage or change in dosage form

According to CCSA, if OIG had used Yellow Book standards in 2015, these issues would not have arisen. Therefore, CCSA requests the bill be amended to require that the OIG use only Yellow Book standards

The California Medical Association (CMA), writes that to comply with both the Framework and federal regulations, physicians are heavily reliant on their EHR vendors. For example, if a practice decides to implement the Framework by contracting with a health information organization (HIO), they will need their vendor to work with the HIO to develop an interface that facilitates the flow of data. That interface may be unique to the practice. CMA explains the problem arises when the vendors take advantage of situations and then charge unreasonable fees to the practice to develop the interface. These fees can range into the tens of thousands of dollars per physician. Because the state requires compliance with the Framework, physicians face a choice to pay the fees, break state law, or change EHR vendors. CMA states any of the above can cause massive disruption for the practice and its patients. This bill addresses the issues mentioned above by empowering the DxF advisory group to develop standards for including EHR vendors, requiring EHR vendors to sign the DxF, incorporating federal standards for reasonableness of vendor fees into state statute, and authorizing the state to enforce these standards

The Department of Social Services (DSS) and the California Welfare Director's Association (CWDA) express concerns that verification of a homestudy report conducted under different standards and methods than those set by California law would be problematic. Because a social worker is required to review and verify the homestudy report as part of the adoption process, the CWDA and DSS are concerned with the potential increased expense of sending a social worker to a foreign country to verify the accuracy of such a homestudy. There are questions as to who would shoulder the costs associated with the social worker's time, travel, and other expenses. The author has offered an amendment that would enable a homestudy report to be conducted according to internationally uniform procedures as established in 1993 by the Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Co-operation in with respect to intercountry adoption [hereafter Hague Convention]. , lines 27 to 35 would be amended to read: (d) If a petitioner is not a resident of California or of the United States, an updated and current homestudy report, conducted and approved by a licensed adoption agency or other authorized resource in the state or country that is a member of the Hague Convention in which the petitioner resides, shall be reviewed and endorsed by the department or delegated county adoption agency, if the standards and criteria established for a homestudy report in the other state or country are substantially commensurate with the homestudy standards and criteria established in California adoption regulations. c The Hague Convention provides for an evaluation similar to a homestudy Article 13 of the Hague Convention requires that a report be submitted to the state of origin including information about the prospective adoptive parents' identity, eligibility and suitability to adopt, background, family and medical history, social environment, reasons for adoption, ability to undertake an intercountry adoption, as well as the characteristics of the children for whom they would be qualified to care. The Hague Convention provides a procedural structure much like the Interstate Compact for the Placement of Children provides for the safe transfer, supervision, and potential recovery of a child pending adoption in the United States. The Convention governs all intercountry adoptions that become parties to it and sets minimum standards and procedures between implementing countries to safeguard adopted children from: abduction, sale, or trafficking of children

The existing CalPERS DB pension plan is a strong tool in recruiting a highly skilled workforce because it attracts already highly skilled employees seeking protection from market risk and the guarantee of a lifetime allowance upon retirement. These employees are willing to forgo higher salary from the state's private sector or public agency competitors for the security inherent in the state's DB plan. However, this bill creates a type of adverse selection that may weaken the DB plan because by offering the ability to opt out of the DB together with the ability to opt in after completing 5 years of employment, new employees with little intention or certainty of staying long term will by default opt out of the DB plan knowing that if they do end up staying long term they have another chance to join CalPERS and if they do not, they can take a portion or all of the employer contribution with them depending on when they leave. Currently, if an employee leaves before retiring and chooses to withdraw his or her employee contributions, the employer contributions stay in the PERF to help reduce costs to providing pensions to employees who remain and complete their career with the state

A penal statute must define the offense with sufficient precision that "ordinary people can understand what conduct is prohibited and in a manner that does not encourage arbitrary and discriminatory enforcement." (United States v. Lanier (1997) 520 U.S. 259, PageG 265.) This bill provides two definitions for "state employees" for purposes of the bill's provisions. It is unclear whether the ability to opt out of the CalPERS DB pension applies only to new employees pursuant to the first definition or "includes" all employees, as specified, under the second definition. The committee assumes that the bill is intended only to permit new state employees to opt out of the DB plan and the second definition is intended to identify the categories of state employees from which new employees may be covered under this bill. However, the committee recommends consolidating and clarifying the two definitions into one definition. Otherwise, certain provisions of the bill may apply to more than just new state employees. If that occurred, there would be significant difficulties related to conflicting provisions with respect to CalPERS membership status, vested rights, mixed DB/ DC service, et al
This bill raises significant questions regarding how an employee who opts out of the DB plan and chooses the DC plan will be covered for the state's active member health benefits, disability benefits, death and survivor benefits, and post-retirement health coverage, which are all dependent on CalPERS membership. The bill makes no provisions for replacing these programs for an employee who opts out of CalPERS. The bill would also defease the employee of the right to reciprocity with other public agencies, as well as COLAs on the employee's retirement allowance

This bill would allow authorized representatives of any news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network to enter areas that have been closed by law enforcement due to a demonstration, march, protest or rally, including the immediate area surrounding any emergency field command post or any other command post. This bill would, additionally, prohibit a peace officer from intentionally assaulting, interfering with or obstructing these duly authorized representatives who are gathering, receiving or processing information for communication to the public. Media access to public gatherings - especially protests - is essential for a functioning democracy, and law enforcement should not be able to interfere with those efforts. But I am concerned that this legislation too broadly defines a "duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network." As written, this bill would allow any person who appears to be engaged in gathering, receiving or processing information, who produces a business card, press badge, other similar credential, or who is carrying professional broadcasting or recording equipment, to have access to a restricted law enforcement area. This could include those individuals who may pose a security risk - such as white nationalists, extreme anarchists or other fringe groups with an online presence

This bill would require firearms to be securely to the vehicle's frame using a steel cable lock or chain permanently affixed to the vehicle. In research conducted by the Alameda County District Attorney's Office, we discovered that between 2012 and 2017, law enforcement agencies across the state reported to the California Department of Justice, Automated Firearms System (AFS) 83,695 firearms stolen and 1,520 as lost. This data demonstrates that proper storage of firearms must be a high priority for our Legislature. Current law only mandates the proper storage of just a 'handgun' in an unattended vehicle. This bill would include all firearms including rifles, shotguns or assault weapons which are common types of weapons that are used by both law enforcement and law abiding citizens. Current law also does not address that if the handgun is locked in a container out of view, the whole container can be stolen. Current law also states that the handgun can be locked in the trunk but most trunks are easily accessible through the passenger compartment. This bill would additionally require the firearm to be secured to the vehicle's frame using a steel cable lock or chain that is permanently affixed to the vehicle

Unfortunately, because our Penal Code's sentencing provisions are so prolix, courts sometimes overlooked this fairly new, and obscure, statute. While we support the creation of reintegration credits for parolees, we oppose this bill's exclusion of all persons required to register pursuant to Section 290 from that potential benefit....The fact is that registrants have an extremely low rate of re-offense and are unlikely to commit a new sex offense in any location. Specifically, the actual rate of re-offense for a registrant on parole is less than one percent, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's Outcome Evaluation Report issued in August 2016 (see p. 31.) In addition, the current language of the bill is too broad because the bill's exclusion could be interpreted to include parolees whose current conviction is not based on a sex offense, but who was convicted of a sex offense decades ago. Under this interpretation, the law could be found to violate the Equal Protection clause of the federal and state constitutions because it would have disparate impact upon state parolees

Writing in support of the bill, Sustainable Conservation notes its organization partners with researchers across the state, including UC ANR and its associated cooperative extensions, as well as growers and other stakeholders, to develop "new and sustainable practices to help meet the state's climate resilience and water conservation goals." These practices that are aimed at managing the impact of greenhouse gases from dairy manure management include reducing nitrate loading through subsurface drip irrigation technology, cover cropping for both soil health and water supply benefits, and other innovations. Sustainable Conservation contends this bill, by expanding the network of research farms to continue this kind of groundbreaking work, will provide additional investment in the kind of innovation that is needed to respond to the ongoing climate crisis

Hague Convention pending federal implementation The Convention was established in 1993 and has been ratified by more than 45 countries, including the United States. Congress passed the implementing legislation in 2000. However, ratification of the Treaty will not occur until the final implementing regulations are completed and the documents are deposited with the Hague. As of April 2003, the draft regulations are pending review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). Thereafter the regulations will be submitted for public comment and be revised before final adoption. The implementation date of the Convention by the federal government is expected to happen in 2004. 4. This bill may be premature: suggested amendment would postpone implementation Given that the federal implementation of the Hague Convention and subsequent federal regulations have not yet been developed, the CWDA argues that is premature. Although the CWDA has not taken a position on the bill, they are concerned about the potential safety risks to children and the need to ensure that all safeguards are in place to secure their protection abroad. The CWDA suggests that the bill be amended to direct DSS to develop regulations that provide the needed protection for prospective adopted California children. The CWDA believes that is in the best interest of these children to wait for these federal instructions to be developed prior to the state developing its own regulations in order to be consistent with the final federal regulations and the intent of the Convention. Article 2.1 GC Sections 21078, 21078.1, 21078.2, 21078.3, 21078.4 - State Peace Officers' and Firefighters' Defined Contribution Plan The Unit 6 agreement would establish a defined contribution plan under the Public Employees' Retirement system (PERS). The purpose of the plan is to supplement the employer-provided pension benefits. Employer contributions and employee contributions, at rates yet to be determined, would be made to the "State Peace Officer/Firefighter Defined Contribution Plan". Employee contributions would be made on a pre-tax basis and be subject to the limitations prescribed by the Internal Revenue Code -- i.e. $30,000 or 25% of compensation, whichever is less, is the maximum which can be annually contributed to this type of plan. This limitation includes the amount of employer and employee contributions going into this plan and participation in, for example, the 401(k) program in the State's Saving Plus Program. Employee accounts will be invested by PERS, and accounts will be credited with earnings at the net earnings rate. Administrative costs will be deducted from the members' accounts. At retirement or death, the member or survivor could elect to take a lump sum or an annuity payment from the remaining balance. 22822 Permanent Intermittent Employees - Health Benefits Adds supercession language to the provision providing eligible permanent intermittent employees a choice to enroll or not enroll in health benefits

Enforcement mechanism To encourage enforcement of the above investor protections, this bill would allow a person who purchases securities in an offering that fails to meet all of the terms and conditions of this bill to bring an action, as specified, for the rescission of the purchase. The bill would also provide that in addition to the other remedies, as specified, the court shall award attorney's fees and costs to a prevailing purchaser in any such action. a. Attorney's fees Generally, in the United States, the "American rule" is that parties must bear their own costs of civil litigation. In Alyeska Pipeline Co. v. Wilderness Society (1975) 421 U.S. 240, the United States Supreme Court held that it was the province of the legislative branch to craft exceptions to the American rule, and courts were not free to shift such costs absent express legislative authorization. (Id. at 269-270.) In this situation where the investor has been defrauded out of potentially devastating amounts of money and the cost of litigation can be cost-prohibitive given the nature of the action, it does not appear unreasonable to allow for attorney's fees where the investor prevails. This is particularly true where the potential harm is not limited to one individual - it is likely that a person misusing this exemption has harmed or may harm other parties. By litigating the issue, therefore, it arguably does provide a significant benefit to the general public in prohibiting further abuse of the securities market by that issuer. b. Contract rescission remedy In addition to the above allowance for attorney's fees, this bill would permit a person who purchases securities in an offering that fails to meet all of the terms and conditions of this bill to bring an action, as specified, for rescission of the purchase. With respect to the contract rescission provision in this bill, that right is already one afforded to individuals under several sections of the Corporate Securities Law of 1968. For example, Section 25401 makes it unlawful for any person to offer or sell a security in this state or buy or offer to buy a security in this state by means of a communication which includes an untrue statement of a material fact or omits to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, as specified. Under Section 25501, where such violation occurs, the sale is subject to rescission, or if the plaintiff or defendant no longer owns the security in question the latter is liable in damages, unless the defendant proves that the plaintiff knew the facts concerning the untruth or omission or that the defendant exercised reasonable care and did not know (or if he had exercised reasonable care would not have known) of the untruth or omission. Moreover, Civil Code Section 1689 provides for contract rescission by a party to the contract in specified cases, including, among others: (1) where the consent of the party rescinding was given by mistake, or obtained through duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence, as specified

Intervenor Rights and Compensation. Should the right of the public to ointerveneo in CEA proceedings be limited solely to oratemakingo matters? Generally, intervenors are allowed broad latitude to challenge a host of insurance activities that adversely affect consumers. Also, in normal proceedings intervenors are compensated for their participation by the insurer seeking to raise rates -- but not in this case. There is a component of the DOI budget for compensating intervenors in general regulatory matters before the DOI. Should funds set aside to assist public intervention in matters related to the regulation by the DOI of private insurer activities be diverted to CEA activities? 12. Amendments to meet IRS conditions? Recently, the IRS has provided a so-called oadvice lettero to the Commissioner, opining that the CEA is structured in such a manner as to qualify for otax-exempt status.o However, the letter is effectively a conditional endorsement. The IRS did not place explicit conditions or demand specific changes in order to reach the conclusion that the CEA qualifies for favorable tax treatment. Instead, it produced an analysis of the CEA as proposed, discussed a range of features, including a number of assumptions, and concluded that, based on that analysis, tax-exempt status would be appropriate. (, lines 20-23.) The Natural Resources Committee may wish to consider whether or not it is appropriate to require DFG to submit proposals to the Committee prior to receiving approval by the Governor, and in general if this is the appropriate relationship between the regulating agency and the industry that is supposed to be regulated. 3) The previous program established by Section 1068 of the Fish and Game Code to promote education and communication within the sea urchin industry explicitly provided that DFG's overhead costs and expenses were to be covered by the funds collected from the landing tax, provided that the amount did not exceed 15% of the revenues collected. On of the bill, subdivision (c) provides that 15% of the revenues generated by the landing tax may be used to "administer the programs or projects funded pursuant to subdivision (b)" but it is unclear if this refers to DFG or the Committee. Presumably, it refers to DFG. In addition, subdivision (b) only directs the Committee to recommend potential expenditures to DFG, and allows DFG and the Committee to jointly establish a formal grant program. Therefore, subdivision (c) could be read to only cover the administrative costs of those specific programs or activities recommended by the Committee, and not those undertaken by DFG. The committee staff recommends the following technical amendments on of the bill: Line 33, after the word "used" insert the words, "to cover departmental overhead charges, and" (Staff note: this phrase is lifted from current Section 1068) Line 34, strike the words "pursuant to subdivision (b)" and insert "by the department,". 4 On , lines 34-39, DFG is required to assign an employee to staff the Committee and "ensure the actions of the committee are carried out and its recommendations appropriately considered by the department?" The bill is silent as to how DFG will cover the cost of reassigning this employee, and exactly what this DFG staff person must do in order to ensure that DFG "appropriately consider(s" the Committee's recommendations in light of the fact that the coordinator will still be an employee of DFG. If the suggested amendment from 3 above is adopted, staff also recommends the following: On , lines 37-38, strike the words "carried out and its recommendations appropriately considered by" and insert "communicated to

more contingent capital of oup to $2 billiono which can be called by the CEA if all of its other resources have been depleted. However, the two different layers of contingent capital are strengthened by by deletion of the orun-offo language contained in AB 13 which reduced the insurer obligation over time. Nonetheless, this does not answer the question of whether an industry contribution of oup to $6 billiono is adequate in the first place. A representative of the DOI testified at an Insurance Committee hearing on the CEA that the $6 billion amount was arrived at simply because it was the most the Commissioner could get the industry to agree to. However, Consumers Union notes other reasons why this amount may not be sufficient. It points out that Commissioner Quackenbush repeated several times at the first hearing on the proposal that each of the layers totaling $12.5 billion would be critical to the financial viability of the CEA. However, the current proposal contains only a $10.5 billion maximum level due to the deletion of a potential $2 billion opolicyholder assessmento layer. Neither increased insurer contributions nor an enhancement of any of the other layers of financing have backfilled this $2 billion hole. In comparison to the CEAos oup to $6 billiono insurer contribution, Florida is considering an industry cap on hurricane exposure in the $20 billion range. Is the financial obligation on the industry sufficient either in terms of adequacy of CEA financing, or in terms of adequate insurer contribution for the benefits obtained? Should the bill be amended to increase the level of insurer contribution by at least another $2 billion to return to the originally proposed $12.5 billion total? 7. Higher Rates for CEA policies. The average CEA rate will be $3.29 per $1000 of insured value. The rating plan provides for average rates in the various rating territories from close to $1 per $1000 in low-risk zones to $5.25 per $1000 higher risk zones. However, there are variations of these averages even within the various rating territories. For instance, older homes and homes which are not wood frame construction pay significantly more than the average within any particular rating territory. Consumer groups have pointed out that the private insurers which have filed rates for ono-frillso earthquake policies, and the reports concerning rates to be charged by the FAIR Plan for its ono-frillso policy, are significantly lower than CEA rates. They argue that this rate comparison, in and of itself, is a strong reason for consumers to resist the costly CEA proposal. The CEA rates estimated to date are premised on the coverage described in AB 13. However, with the additional coverages provided by , it is clear that CEA rates would rise even further and be even less attractive in comparison to alternative private insurer and FAIR Plan ono frillso policies. The rates for CEA policies are higher than private sector alternatives because the CEA faces costs not imposed on private insurers. For a start-up, mono-line, government-run insurance company writing only a catastrophic risk, long term rate adequacy is not sufficient. Because catastrophic events are unpredictable, the CEA may need to pay out claims in the short term that would otherwise require several years of accumulation to fund. It therefore needs to obuy,o at substantial cost, immediate protection (in the case of the CEA, large amounts of oreinsuranceo and expensive ocapital marketo securities) to cover short term exposure. Private insurers, on the other hand, have existing capital and surplus from all lines, and they have premium income from all lines, and can rely on these resources to protect against short-term catastrophic losses. As a result, long term rate adequacy appears to be lower for these private companies than for the CEA. 8. Meeting the preconditions established by AB 13. The bill states that the Commissioner has met the AB 13 requirement that he obtain commitments of at least 75% of the insurer market before returning to the Legislature to obtain authorization to commence CEA operations. However, the Commissioner has reported that he has actually obtained commitments from only 70% of the market. Should the bill be amended to condition authorization for the CEA to commence operations on obtaining the full 75% participation which the Commissioner has indicated is necessary? The bill does not state that commitments for $ 1.5 billion of capital market financing have been obtained as required by AB 13. The author indicates that it is simply impossible to obtain o commitmentso (the operative word in AB 13) for the capital market layer of financing, given the manner in which these securities must be marketed. However, it should be noted that the Treasurer and the financial houses with whom the CEA has contracted to market these securities believe that adequate markets exist for this layer of financing. Should the bill be amended to condition authorization for the CEA to commence operations on obtaining $1.5 billion in some form of capital market financing? 9. Bondholder preference over policyholders for premium revenue. The revenue bonds issued by the CEA were designed under AB 13 to be supported by CEA policyholder surcharges. now adds that all revenues, including premiums, shall be owed first to bondholders. Should policyholder premiums be dedicated to retiring investor bonds in preference to claims payments? Will this provision increase the likelihood of pro rata payouts to homeowners? Does this change make the CEA more of an investment vehicle than an insurance program? 10. Condominium coverage.
